blocks.text: Pliny, book 10, chapter 23: From what place storks come, or where they betake themselves, is not yet known. That they come from far away is not in doubt, in the same manner as cranes. See the rest there. Solinus, chapter 40: Pythonos Come in Asia is a place of open plains, where at the time of their first arrival the storks fly together and tear to pieces the one that came last. (Just as Caesar reports that among the Gauls, whoever had come last to the council was customarily subjected to every kind of torture and put to death in the sight of the multitude.) Aelian, History, book 3, chapter 23: Προακούω δὲ τοὺς πελαργοὺς καὶ αὐταῖς συμφεύγειν ταῖς γεράνοις, καὶ συναποδιδράσκειν τὸν χειμῶνα· τῆς δὲ ὥρας τῆς κρυμώδους διελθούσης ὅταν ὑποστρέφωσιν εἰς τὰ ἴδια, καὶ οἵδε καὶ αἵδε, τὴν ἑαυτῶν ἕκαστος καλιὰν ἀναγνωρίζουσιν, ὡς τὴν οἰκίαν ἄνθρωποι [Proakouō de tous pelargous kai autais sympheugein tais geranois, kai synapodidraskein ton cheimōna; tēs de hōras tēs krymōdous dielthousēs hotan hypostrephōsin eis ta idia, kai hoide kai haide, tēn heautōn hekastos kalian anagnōrizousin, hōs tēn oikian anthrōpoi]. I also hear that storks flee with the cranes and depart together with them in winter; and that, when the cold is over, both these and those, migrating back to their native abode, each recognize their own nests as men recognize their home. Accordingly they hold that the Pelasgians, διὰ τὸ πλανήτας εἶναι, καὶ δίκην ὀρνέων ἐπιφοιτᾷν ἐφ᾽ οὓς ἔτυχε τόπους, Πελαργοὺς ὑπὸ τῶν Ἀττικῶν κληθῆναι [dia to planētas einai, kai dikēn orneōn epiphoitan eph' hous etyche topous, Pelargous hypo tōn Attikōn klēthēnai], because they were wanderers and roamed into any places whatever like storks, were called Pelargoi by the Athenians. So Strabo in book 5; and again in book 9: Ὑπὸ τῶν Ἀττικῶν Πελαργοὶ προσηγορεύθησαν διὰ τὴν πλάνην [Hypo tōn Attikōn Pelargoi prosēgoreuthēsan dia tēn planēn], On account of their wanderings they were called Pelargoi by the Athenians. (Although in the Etymologicum some prefer that they were so called διὰ τὰς σινδόνας, ἃς ἐφόρουν [dia tas sindonas, has ephoroun], on account of the garments they wore, marked like storks with black and [III, 92] white.) II. Many of the Fathers assert the same of storks. Thus Basil writes in Homily 8: Κατὰ τὸν ἕνα καιρὸν πάντας ἐπιδημεῖν τοῖς τῇ δε χωρίοις, οὕτω δὲ ὑφ᾽ ἑνὶ συνθήματι πάντας ἀπαίρειν [Kata ton hena kairon pantas epidēmein tois tē de chōriois, houtō de hyph' heni synthēmati pantas apairein], All make for these places at one time, and likewise all depart as if at one given signal. Which Eustathius imitates thus in the Hexaëmeron: Οἱ δὲ πελαργοὶ καὶ ἑνὶ ἐπιδημοῦσι συνθήματι, καὶ ἑνὶ ἀπαίρουσι [Hoi de pelargoi kai heni epidēmousi synthēmati, kai heni apairousi]. And Ambrose: They say that storks set out in a gathered troop, if they think they must go anywhere, and arrive together in many places around the East, and all move in unison as if at a military watchword. And Isidore: These heralds of spring, companions in fellowship, enemies of serpents, fly across the seas and proceed to Asia in a gathered troop. III. The Arabs and Hebrews too. Alkazuinius: لا يزال يتبع الربيع وله وكران احدهما بالجروم والاخر بالصرود ولا يزال يتحول من احدهما الي الاخر [lā yazālu yatbaʿu al-rabīʿ wa-lahu wakrān aḥaduhumā bi-l-jurūm wa-l-ākhar bi-l-ṣurūd wa-lā yazālu yataḥawwalu min aḥadihimā ilā al-ākhar] It never ceases to follow the spring; and, since it has two nests, one for summer and the other for winter, it does not cease to migrate from the one to the other. Damir from Avicenna: من ذكاه انه يتخذ له عشين يسكن في واحد منهما بعض وانه اذا احسن يتغير الهوا [min dhakāhu annahu yattakhidhu lahu ʿushshayn yaskunu fī wāḥid minhumā baʿḍ wa-annahu idhā aḥsana yataghayyaru al-hawā] It belongs to its cleverness that it has two nests, in one of which it dwells for some (supply الزمان [al-zamān] time, that is, for a while) and, when it is convenient, it changes air. Kimchi on Jeremiah: החסידה מנהגה לשכון [col. 332] בימי הקור והחורף במקום אחר ובימי הקיץ והחום במקום אחר, In the time of cold and winter the stork is wont to dwell in one place, and in another in the days of summer and heat. IV. More recent writers. Caspar Heldelinus: On the Ides of August the storks, young and old, in a most beautiful gathered troop, enter upon that laborious journey by night under the moon. But before they cross the sea, all those that our fields have sent forth gather at the Athesis, a river of Gaul, not very far from the Sextinian waters (for Sextinianis read Sextiis), or, as others prefer, the Sestian altars, namely where Marius routed the Cimbri with the sword. There, holding public assemblies among themselves, they murmur together, review the army, etc. Moreover, when about to depart, they prudently wait for a favourable north wind; and as soon as it blows more steadily, then, as if on a day fixed by law, they hasten their departure. Belon: When I was near Abydos, on 24 August, I saw a huge multitude of storks, which seemed to come to three or four thousand. They were flying from Russia and Tartary, and were crossing the Hellespont transversely in a crisscross formation. And when they were above Tenedos, they wheeled about in a long winding course until they were all gathered into a circle. Then, before going farther from the mouth of the Propontis, they divided themselves into some smaller squadrons, more than twenty, and followed one another toward the South. Since, therefore, storks depart and return at fixed times, the Prophet rightly said: The stork [III, 93] in the heaven knoweth her times. Kimchi understands by the stork in the heaven the stork that nests in a high place, בישוב במגדלי הגבוהים ובמדבר בעצים הגבוהים, namely on the highest towers, if the places are inhabited; or in the loftiest trees, if they are deserted; as it is said in the Psalm, The firs are her house. So Deut. I, 28. and IX, 1.: Cities great and fortified בשמים, in heaven, that is, up to heaven. And Prov. XXX, 19.: The way of an eagle in the heaven, that is, which flies upward. Yet, since the stork's nest is not in question here, I prefer to interpret thus: the stork in the heaven, that is, in the air, and from the air, knows the time of its migration, and that it must depart when the air grows warm and the cold abates.
